blocks.text: Compounds in which a hydroxyl group is bonded to an arene called phenols. The chemical formula of the simplest phenol is C₆H₅OH. Phenol is also known as carbolic acid and was used as carbolic soap. Phenol is a crystalline white solid. Some examples of phenols are given below:

blocks.alt: Three structures: phenol, a benzene ring with OH; 2-naphthol, two fused rings with OH at position 2; 1-naphthol, two fused rings with OH at position 1.
blocks.caption: Examples of phenols: phenol, 2-naphthol and 1-naphthol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 95).

blocks.text: Phenols can be produced by the reaction of phenylamine with nitrous acid (HNO₂). The nitrous acid used here is produced in situ. The reaction occurs in three steps.

items: Step 1 - The HNO₂ is so unstable that it needs to be prepared in a test-tube by reacting sodium nitrite (NaNO₂) and dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl) while keeping the temperature below 10°C using ice.
Step 2 - Phenylamine is then reacted with the HNO₂ to form an unstable diazonium salt
Step 3 - On further warming, phenol is produced as diazonium salt is decomposed (hydrolysed).

blocks.alt: Phenylamine (benzene ring with NH2), with NaNO2 over the arrow and 'HCl, < 10 degrees C' under it, gives benzenediazonium chloride (ring with N+ triple bond N and Cl-), which with H2O over the arrow and 'warm' under it gives phenol + N2 + HCl.
blocks.caption: Preparation of phenol from phenylamine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 95, with the last step corrected).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed scheme uses NaOH for the last step and gives phenol + NaCl + N2. Phenol is made by warming the diazonium salt solution with water: C6H5N2+ Cl- + H2O -> C6H5OH + N2 + HCl, as drawn above and as the book itself gives in Chapter 24 (PDF page 125). In alkali the phenol would form phenoxide and couple with the remaining diazonium ions to give an azo dye.
